paras: Ten years ago a woman in Porto Alegre started doing something small on the last Sunday of December. She opens a notebook and writes three headings across a page: what I stopped doing, what I started doing, and what I kept doing even when it was hard. It takes about forty minutes. She has never missed a year, and she says the notebook has changed more decisions than any plan she has ever written.

The first column is easy and slightly embarrassing. It is where you find out how much you gave up without ever deciding to. “You do not remember stopping,” she says. “You end up not doing it, which is a different verb altogether. Nobody chooses to stop running. You miss a Tuesday, and then a week, and then you have not been for a year and you cannot help feeling that somebody took it from you.”

The second column is where she says people lie, and she includes herself. It fills up with things you intend to do and things you have contemplated doing, and almost none of them survive to the following December. Her rule now is that nothing goes into that column unless it has already happened four times.

The third column is the one she says is worth keeping the notebook for. It is short, it is boring, and it is the only honest page in the book. “What you persisted in is who you are,” she says. “Not what you committed to in January, and not what you dedicated yourself to for three weeks. What you were still doing in October, when nobody was watching and it was not interesting any more.” Two years ago she resumed something she had stopped at twenty-three. It is in the third column now, which took longer than it sounds, because she hesitated to write it down until she was sure.
reading.source: A composite portrait of an annual habit, written for this lesson.

items.situation: Say one thing you gave up, using the verb that always takes -ing.
tips: Give up is in the -ing group. Never gave up to play.

items.situation: Say one thing you intend to do this year.
tips: I intend to take the exam in November.
Intend is in the to group.

items.situation: Now say the difference between I stopped playing and I stopped to think.
tips: I stopped playing means I quit.
I stopped to think means I paused in order to think. Two different sentences.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: I am looking forward to see the result.
tips: I am looking forward to seeing the result.
That to is a preposition, so it takes -ing.

items.situation: Say something you ended up not doing this year.
tips: I ended up not going to the gym on weekdays.
End up always takes -ing, and the negative goes before it.

items.situation: Say one thing you kept doing when it stopped being interesting.
tips: I kept watching series in English even when I was too tired to follow them.
Keep is in the -ing group, and this is your third column.

listenings.text: The entry I am proudest of took me two years to write down, and it is three words long. I stopped playing the piano at twenty-three, and I did not decide to. I just ended up not doing it, one week at a time, until it had been eight years. Then I resumed it, badly, at thirty-one. And for two whole Decembers I hesitated to put it in the third column, because the third column is for things you kept, and I was afraid of writing something I would have to remove the following year. Last December I finally wrote it, and I cannot help thinking that the two years of not writing it were the actual work. Anybody can start again in January. Deserving the third column takes longer.

We asked four hundred people to name the date they stopped doing something they used to do every week. Almost nobody could. What they could name, in extraordinary detail, was the day they started. That asymmetry tells you something about how the mind handles beginnings and endings. A beginning is a decision, so it gets stored as an event. An ending is usually not a decision at all. It is the eleventh missed Tuesday, and there is nothing to store. So when people tell me they gave something up, I ask a slightly rude question: did you give it up, or did you end up not doing it? The second one is much more common and it is much easier to reverse, because there is no decision standing in the way. You are not going back on anything. You are just resuming.
